Stirring-based control strategy for microaerobic H2S removal in sequencing 
batch anaerobic digesters 
M. Andreides *,1, L. Pokorn´a-Krayzelov´a 2, J. Bart´aˇckov´a 3, J. Bart´aˇcek 4 
Department of Water Technology and Environmental Engineering, University of Chemistry and Technology Prague, Technick´a 5, 166 28 Prague 6, Czech Republic   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Anaerobic digestion 
Biomethane, Hydrogen sulfide 
Mathematical modelling 
Microaeration 
Stirring intensity 
A B S T R A C T   
Microaeration in fermenters is challenging due to the rapid increase of H2S concentration upon the start of 
stirring, which makes biogas utilization less attractive. On these occasions, apparent H2S production exceeds the 
ability of sulfur-oxidizing bacteria (SOB) to remove H2S, which results in peak H2S concentrations in biogas. This 
study shows that such peaks can be reduced by stirring optimization. For the first time, the effect of the stirring 
intensity on microaeration was evaluated in a lab-scale sequencing batch reactor and supported by a biokinetic 
mathematical model. Single stirring intensity (15, 25, 35, and 55 RPM) and gradually increasing stirring intensity 
(15 to 35 RPM) were compared. Despite achieving a stably low concentration of H2S in the fermenter at low 
stirring speed, the accumulation of volatile fatty acids in liquid occurred. However, with gradually increasing 
stirring intensity, slower stirring at the beginning of the cycle led to the slower release of H2S, thereby, winning 
more time for SOB to remove H2S from biogas. H2S peaks were reduced by this strategy and no accumulation of 
volatile fatty acids in the liquid phase was observed. Since microaeration is zero-waste chemical-free desulfur­
ization method, its optimization and H2S peaks reduction can help to expand its use.   
1. Introduction 
Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is an inevitable poisonous product of the 
anaerobic digestion of sulfur-rich substrates [12]. Burning biogas 
contaminated with H2S shortens the lifetime of cogeneration units and 
increases operational costs due to the corrosion of concrete and steel 
structures. Also, when the biogas is upgraded to biomethane and 
injected into the natural gas distribution grid, H2S concentrations must 
be negligible, typically below 5 ppm [5]. 
Complete desulfurization of biogas can be expensive, especially 
when treating biogas significantly contaminated with H2S (thousands of 
ppm). Moreover, often used technologies such as alkaline wash or 
filtration on activated carbon require waste disposal or regeneration 
[15]. On the other hand, well-controlled microaeration can serve as a 
great zero-waste chemical-free method for biogas pre-treatment with 
subsequent post-treatment of residual H2S concentrations on e.g., acti­
vated carbon filters. 
Microaeration is a well-known biological method for the removal of 
H2S from biogas directly in anaerobic digesters [12]. It is achieved by 
dosing small amount of oxygen or air into the anaerobic fermenter 
(typically into the headspace) to support the growth of sulfide oxidizing 
bacteria (SOB). SOB present in the biofilm colonizing the surfaces of 
reactor’s headspace oxidize H2S to harmless elemental sulfur [17]. Even 
though microaeration is commonly used in full-scale applications, there 
are still significant drawbacks associated with fermenters that are 
intermittently stirred, which may disqualify this biotechnology espe­
cially when biogas is upgraded to biomethane. 
Intermittently mixed microaerated fermenters often experience 
peaks of H2S concentrations in the headspace immediately after the start 
of stirring, resulting in insufficient biological oxidation. Similar peaks 
are observed when the substrate is dosed discontinuously [3]. This 
phenomenon is explained as a rapid release of H2S from liquid after the 
start of the stirring. The typical response from operators to such peak 
production is the upregulation of dose air leading to biogas overloading

with nitrogen and subsequent above-limit emissions of NOx upon 
burning in a cogeneration unit [6]. Furthermore, H2S peaks also increase 
the operational costs of biogas upgrading to biomethane. As a result, 
reducing the H2S peaks and maintaining H2S concentration on stably 
low levels without polluting or diluting the biogas by oxygen or air is a 
major challenge. 
Intermittent stirring is often favorable choice for operators since it is 
robust, saves energy costs and can improve biogas production [20]. In 
reactors with intermittent stirring, biogas production as well as H2S 
concentration in biogas rapidly increases after stirring starts. Stafford 
[21] tested different stirring intensities to prove, that biogas release 
after the start of mixing is higher than later during the mixing phase. 
However, the stirring regime can also significantly affect e.g. volatile 
fatty acid production, methane production, biogas composition, micro­
bial population dynamics, or sheer stress [20]. Therefore, it is necessary 
to carefully adjust stirring intensity and monitor its effect on the entire 
anaerobic digestion process. 
In our previous study, a new mathematical model of microaeration in 
SBR suggested that the intensity of stirring largely affected the H2S 
release from liquid during operational cycle [3]. Therefore, we hy­
pothesized that controlled release of H2S from liquid due to proper 
stirring control can win more time for biological oxidation in the 
headspace and thereby significantly improve the efficiency of 
microaeration. 
In this lab-scale study, we experimentally tested various stirring re­
gimes of microaerated SBR, including different constant stirring in­
tensities and gradually increased stirring intensity, to eliminate the H2S 
concentration peaks in headspace. Consequently, we developed an 
optimal stirring-control strategy that assured a complete reduction of 
H2S peaks. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Set-up configuration 
To study the effect of mixing intensity on microaeration efficiency, 
two laboratory acrylic glass reactors (experimental reactor R, and con­
trol reactor C) were build and operated for 360 days. Reactors were 
operated under mesophilic conditions (44 ◦C) and the volume of each 
reactor was 20 L including 13 L of sludge and 7 L of headspace. To 
maintain consistent influent composition, both reactors were fed by 
artificial substrate: cheese whey solution (40 g L-1) with the addition of 
K2SO4 (1.8 g L-1) to increase the amount of H2S in the biogas. The ho­
mogenization of the sludge was ensured with a two-blade impeller. Pure 
oxygen was dosed continuously into the headspace of both reactors (4 
mL h−1) using a mass flow controller (Bronkhorst High-Tech B.V., 
Netherlands). Both reactors were operated as sequencing batch reactors 
(SBRs). The sedimentation phase was set to 50 min. The reaction phase 
involved stirring of the sludge and its length was adjusted from 3.5 up to 
8 h based on experiments. After sedimentation, 100 mL of the substrate 
was dosed, and 100 mL of effluent was drained from the reactor 
simultaneously via a double-head peristaltic pump (Watson-Marlow 
Fluid Technology Group, UK). 
The biogas production was measured by gas flow meter Milli­
Gascounters (Dr.-Ing. RITTER Apparatebau GmbH & Co. KG, Germany) 
every 5 min. H2S concentration in biogas was measured by an online H2S 
sensor (H2S/SP-10000, Membrapor, Switzerland) with automatic sam­
pling equipment. The H2S sensor was every 20 min washed with biogas 
for 5 min and then washed with nitrogen for 5 min. According to the 
sensor’s specification datasheet, the resolution of the sensor is less than 
3 ppm and the maximum zero shift is 10 ppm based on the environment 
temperature. This shift was recorded in the results, where the lowest 
measured value corresponds to exactly 10 ppm. 
H2S concentration, temperature, and biogas production measure­
ment were controlled by an in-house program developed using LabVIEW 
2012 software running on a CompactRIO system (National Instruments, 
US) (Fig. 1). 
Sludge from a mesophilic (44 ◦C) anaerobic fermenter (Wastewater 
treatment plant ˇCesk´a Lípa, Czech Republic) was used as inoculum. 
Total suspended solids and volatile suspended solids were 24.5 and 13.8 
g L-1, respectively. 
2.2. Experimental design 
After the inoculation, both reactors were operated without experi­
ments for 9 months to reach steady state in both reactors and to allow 
sufficient time for biofilm growth on the headspace walls under micro­
aerobic conditions. During this phase, stirring speed was 55RPM and the 
reaction phase of SBR took 3.5 h. 
2.2.1. Stirring intensity experiments 
To evaluate the effect of stirring intensity on H2S release from liquid 
and, thus, microaeration efficiency, several experiments were designed. 
The effect of single-speed intensity on the one hand, and gradual 
increasing stirring intensity on the other hand were studied in R. 
First, single-speed experiments were conducted to test four different 
stirring speeds: 15, 25, 35, and 55 RPM. During the experiment, the 
reaction phase was prolonged to from 3.5 to 8 h, to avoid acidification of 
the reactor, which may occur at lower stirring speeds (15 and 25 RPM) 
with reaction time 3.5 h due to the slower degradation of the substrate 
and subsequent accumulation of volatile fatty acids (VFA). 
Secondly, gradual increasing of the stirring intensity within one 
feeding cycle was studied. At the beginning of the cycle, the stirrer speed 
was set to 15 RPM to reduce H2S transfer rate from liquid to gas after 
stirring starts. After two hours, the speed increased to 35 RPM to in­
crease H2S transfer coefficient and to accelerate the release of the rest 
H2S from liquid. The reaction time of these kinetic tests was 4.2 h (250 
min). 
For each single-speed experiment, the intensity was set, and the 
reactor was operated for two-weeks to see the impact of the intensity 
change in long-term. For gradual stirring speed, due to the manual 
switching of the speed requirement, 10 SBR cycles were tested with 
pause, where the speed was set to 35 RPM to see behavior of the system 
while changing stirring regimes. 
2.2.2. Sulfide kinetics in the liquid 
For each single-speed intensity test, kinetics of dissolved sulfide 
concentration in the liquid was measured. During the reaction phase, the 
sludge was sampled every hour and the concentration of sulfide was 
measured. In the 55-RPM test, the interval between the first two samples 
was shortened to 30 min to catch the peak of the sulfide concentration. 
2.2.3. VFA monitoring 
The overall conditions of the reactors were monitored by volatile 
fatty acids (VFA) concentration measurement since it is one of the most 
important reactor failure indicators [9]. VFA was measured 3 times in 
each intensity test to see potential accumulation. 
2.3. Simulations 
To support experimental results and to verify the functionality of the 
previously developed model [3], simulations in AQUASIM software [19] 
were done. Mathematical model includes 3 compartments: liquid phase, 
headspace, and biofilm. The equilibrium between adjacent compart­
ments was described by Henrýs law. In the model, the faith of sulfur 
substrate was described by seven processes (the uptake of sulfate by SRB 
in the liquid, the chemical oxidation of H2S in the headspace, the uptake 
of H2S by SOB in biofilm, the uptake of S0 by SOB, the decay of SOB, the 
decay of SRB, and washout of H2S from the reactor with the produced 
biogas. For the simulations, the original mathematical model described 
in detail in Andreides et al. [3] was used and retained with the following 
minor modifications:

- The gas-to-biofilm mass transfer coefficient was increased (kLa BF =
50 h−1) since the biofilm area was bigger than in the previous study.  
- The liquid-to-gas mass transfer coefficient kLa value for different 
stirring speed was adjusted to fit experimental data. As the stirring 
speed increased, the kLa value increased. The original kLa value for 
55 RPM was kept at 20 h−1 as determined in the previous study [3].  
- The concentration of sulfate was changed according to the real dose. 
Previously, scenario analyses were done in AQUASIM (Fig. 2) by 
Andreides et al. [3]. It was shown that the change of the stirring speed 
expressed as a change of mass transfer coefficient kLa can significantly 
affect the H2S concentration in the headspace, since the release of H2S 
from liquid can be controlled and the peaks in H2S concentration can be 
thus reduced. In this study, we verified this hypothesis and evaluate the 
real conditions of the system with various tested speed intensities in 
continuously operated lab-scale SBR. 
2.4. Analytical methods 
Every two weeks, the COD concentration of the sludge and effluent 
was measured according to the standard methods [4] and total sus­
pended solids and volatile suspended solids were measured 
gravimetrically. 
For the VFA concentration determination in the liquid phase, a gas 
chromatograph (GC 2010, Shimadzu, Japan) was used and the condi­
tions were set according to Andreides et al. [2]: capillary column CP- 
Vax 58 (25 m length and 0.25 mm ID); flame ionization detector; the 
oven column temperature was set on 70 ◦C; the heating rate of 15 ◦C/ 
min, until it reached 134 ◦C; the injector port and detector temperature 
270 ◦C and 300 ◦C, respectively. The time of the analysis was 5.27 min. 
The analyses of biogas composition (methane, oxygen, nitrogen, and 
carbon dioxide) were performed three times a week at the beginning of 
the reactor’s operation, and later every two weeks since no significant 
change was observed. The analyses were done as in Andreides et al. [3]: 
GC-TCD system (Shimadzu, Japan) with a stainless steel Hayesep D 
packed column (80/100) for biogas composition detection (carbon di­
oxide, methane, air) and a 5A molecular sieve (80/100) for air compo­
sition detection (oxygen, nitrogen): initial temperature of 150 ◦C, 
detector temperature of 185 ◦C, and isocratic analysis at 130 ◦C for both 
columns. Helium was used as the carrier gas, and the analysis time was 3 
and 6 min for biogas and air detection, respectively. 
2.5. Statistical analyses 
For each tested stirring intensities, at least 4 operational cycles were 
performed and the average H2S concentrations and its standard devia­
tion were calculated. To assess the agreement between experimental and 
modeled data, root mean square error (RMSE) was calculated for each 
tested stirring intensity. The mathematical model was fitted to the 
experimental data to find the lowest RMSE. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Overall performance of the reactors 
pH and temperature were stable at 7.2 – 7.4 and 44 ◦C, respectively. 
During off experiment period, the concentration of total VFA in the re­
actors did not exceeded 75 mg L-1 (reaction cycle 3.5 h, 55 RPM). Thus, 
no accumulation of the acids was observed in this phase. 
Biogas composition in reactoŕs headspace was stable during entire 
reactors operation in both reactors (Table 1). 
The concentration of H2S in both reactors fluctuated between values 
close to 0 and approx. 200 ppm after the biofilm development and did 
not exceed 40 ppm, when the gradual stirring was applied. When the 
reactors were operated without microaeration, the concentration in R 
and C was 5800 ± 200 and 5600 ± 300 ppm, respectively. The H2S 
removal efficiency of up to 97% was achieved, which is comparable to 
other studies of microaeration (e.g., [7,10,18].

3.2. Single stirring speed tests 
3.2.1. Comparison of sulfide concentration in the liquid and headspace of 
the digester 
Fig. 3 shows the comparison of sulfide kinetics in the liquid measured 
in prolonged cycles (8 h) with 4 different stirring speeds. Fig. 4 shows 
H2S concentration in the headspace for different stirring speeds. 
At 15 RPM, sulfide concentration increased relatively slowly as H2S 
transfer into biogas was slow. Therefore, H2S oxidation rate in the 
headspace was sufficient and H2S concentration was stable under 80 
ppm. On the other hand, the two-blade impeller used for sludge ho­
mogenization did not ensure a proper homogenization at this low stir­
ring speed, which was demonstrated in a 3D model of Abld et al. [1]. 
Due to the poor homogenization of the sludge, the degradation of 
organic substrate was significantly slower, and the reaction phase had to 
be prolonged to protect anaerobic culture against acidification. This is, 
indeed, not an attractive choice for operators of full-scale digesters. In 
addition, even after 8 h, sulfides were not fully depleted from the sludge 
and, thus, the concentration after the start of stirring was affected by 
residual sulfur compounds concentration from the previous cycle. 
At 25 RPM, the peak of H2S concentration was around 100 ppm. 
When the duration of the reaction phase was kept at 8 h, the conditions 
of the anaerobic sludge were satisfactory, i.e., both VFA and sulfide was 
almost fully depleted from the liquid at the end of the cycle. H2S con­
centration in the next cycle was influenced by minor residual sulfide 
concentration from the previous cycle. 
At 35 RPM, sulfide was depleted from the sludge after 4 h, but the 
H2S concentration in the first hour of the reaction increased above 110 
ppm. Even though the kLa was different with different stirring speeds, 
the highest H2S concentrations during 25 and 35 RPM cycles were very 
similar. This was caused by the different initial sulfide concentration. 
At 55 RPM, sulfide was depleted within one hour. The highest 
concentrations were measured approx. 30 min after the start of mixing. 
As expected, H2S concentration fluctuations were most significant with 
the highest H2S concentrations, reaching almost 140 ppm. 
When the reaction time decreased to 3.5 h, maximum H2S concen­
tration at both 35 and 55 RPM ranged around 200 ppm. 
3.2.2. Monitoring VFA concentration 
For every single-speed intensity (15, 25, 35, 55 RPM) VFA concen­
tration in the reactor was monitored (Table 2) to overview conditions of 
anaerobic culture in the fermenter. 
During the 15-RPM experiment and reaction time 3.5 h, VFA con­
centration went up to 2 g L-1. Even though the VFA inhibition limit 
depends on the buffering capacity of the sludge [16], anaerobic diges­
tion in a full-scale application is considered to be stable when VFA 
concentration does not exceed 1 g L-1 [8]. So, the inhibitory concen­
tration was exceeded with stirring speed 15 RPM, the pH of the reactor 
quickly dropped to 6.4 and as a result, feeding had to be stopped. The 
reaction phase was then prolonged to 8 h to avoid acidification. How­
ever, biogas production did not stop even after 8 h indicating that the 
substrate was not fully degraded yet. To maintain the complete degra­
dation of the substrate, even longer time would be required for 15 and 
25 RPM, which resulted from poor homogenization of the sludge. 
Consequently, organic loading rate significantly decreased, which 
would, in the long term, lead to biomass loss. Therefore, the reaction 
time was not extended beyond 8 h. In all cases mentioned in Table 2, 
acetic acid was the dominant VFA representing up to 80% of all VFA 
produced. 
It is obvious from Table 2, that the higher stirring speed, the lower 
VFA concentration at the end of the cycle. With 55 RPM and reaction 
time 8 h, VFA were almost fully consumed. This phenomenon was also 
shown by Lindmark et al. [13]. During an experiment with 150 RPM, 
VFA consumption was higher compared to 25 RPM and the accumula­
tion of VFA did not occur. On the other hand, too intensive stirring speed 
can lead to a chronic failure of the reactor due to the disruption of 
bacterial structure. Kim et al. [11] operated SBR with stirring speed 300 
RPM which led to a reduced rate of hydrolysis and acidification of the 
reactor. 
Mixing speed of 35 RPM seemed to be the optimal choice for the 
reactor under study, since stable anaerobic digestion could be achieved 
with shorter time than with 15 and 25 RPM and the H2S peaks were 
lower than for 55 RPM. 
To sum up, low stirring speed (15 RPM) was favorable for the effi­
ciency of microaeration, because of the slower H2S release from the 
liquid and, thus the lowest H2S concentration in headspace. However, 
sludge homogenization was not sufficient, the accumulation of VFA 
occurred and pH in the liquid phase start to decrease. Conversely, at 
high stirring speed (55 RPM), anaerobic digestion was stable, but greater 
peaks in H2S concentration in headspace were observed, because of the 
quick desorption of sulfide from the liquid phase. Therefore, to achieve 
both peak reduction and stable anaerobic fermentation, we designed an 
experiment with a gradually increasing stirring intensity. 
3.2.3. The effect of mixing speed on biogas production 
Biogas production was also affected by the intensity of mixing. In 
Fig. 5, three consecutive cycles for each tested stirring intensity are 
compared in terms of biogas production kinetics and total biogas pro­
duction in the individual cycles. In the cycles with higher stirring in­
tensity (35, 55, and gradually increasing stirring intensity), the 
production of biogas per cycle was 1297 ± 53 mL. Biogas productions in 
the cycles with 15 and 25 RPM was 1155 ± 54 mL, which coincides with 
increased VFA concentration (up to 2 mg HAc L-1) remaining in the 
liquid at the end of each cycle. Also, the release of biogas from liquid was 
much slower at 15 and 25 RPM compared to the higher stirring in­
tensities. Both in cycles 35 and 55 RPM, there was a long phase at the 
end of each sample where almost no biogas was produced. The 
composition of biogas was stable in every tested intensity (Tab. 1). 
3.3. Gradually increasing stirring intensity tests 
Fig. 6 shows the comparison between H2S concentration in the 
headspace during SBR cycles with gradual stirring (five cycles, white 
blocks) and single stirring speed (two cycles, grey blocks in the middle). 
When the gradually increasing stirring intensity (15 to 35 RPM) was 
applied, H2S concentration was stable under 40 ppm, peak H2S con­
centrations were reduced, and no VFA accumulation was observed.

When the stirring regime was switched again to single stirring (the 4th 
and 5th cycle in Fig. 6), peak H2S concentrations were observed again. 
Moreover, the reaction time could be decreased to 4 h and 10 min 
while assuring efficient VFA degradation. Here, the stirring intensity 
was changed manually and therefore only two speeds for the gradual 
increasing stirring intensity test were used. When stirring regimes 
switching is automatically controlled and a continuous increase of speed 
is used, the stirring control might be even more effective, and the re­
action time could be even shorter. 
We did not test gradual increase from 15 to 55 RPM due to the 
limitation of the equipment, but, based on the results from H2S and 
sulfate concentration, there is an assumption, that the reaction time 
could be even shorter. In Fig. 6, it is visible that H2S concentration did 
not drop to zero. This phenomenon is probably due to the limitation of 
the H2S sensor mentioned in Chapter 2.1. 
The peak concentrations of H2S were lower with the gradual increase 
of stirring intensity compared to the single stirring speed test with 15 
RPM. As was already mentioned, the residual concentration of sulfide in 
the liquid after the cycles with low stirring intensity can explain this 
phenomenon. On the other hand, when the sulfide depletion was 
reduced by increasing stirring intensity during the cycle, the peak con­
centrations at the beginning of the subsequent cycles (after the start of 
stirring) was reduced. 
3.4. Explaining the experimental results by mathematical model 
The simulation of microaeration with different stirring speeds using 
the mathematical model developed by Andreides et al. [3] is shown in 
Fig. 4A-D. The massive release of H2S at the beginning of the reaction 
phase corresponds to gas release commonly observed in intermittently 
stirred fermenters [21]. Gas release from the liquid phase depends on 
the mass transfer coefficient, which is increased by increasing stirring 
intensity [14]. This assumption served as the basis for the mathematical 
simulation, which showed that H2S release may decrease at lower stir­
ring intensity (Fig. 2). 
In the model developed by Andreides et al. [3] with changing biofilm 
area, only liquid-to-gas mass transfer coefficients kLa and substrate 
concentration was changed to fit the experimental data (Chapter 2.3.). 
The original kLa value derived for 55 RPM in the original mathematical 
model (20 h−1) was changed for other stirring speeds (Fig. 4). Because of

For the simulation of the experiments with gradual stirring speed 
increase (4E), kLa values were used according to Fig. 4. In the first two 
hours, kLa was set to 7 h−1, after two hours the value was increased to 
12 h−1. After 4 h and 10 min, the stirring stopped. In the mathematical 
model, the reactors are considered to be ideally stirred, so, the sedi­
mentation was modeled as an instant drop of kLa to a minimum value. To 
avoid numerical problems in AQUASIM, kLa during sedimentation was 
set to 0.1 h−1. The rapid drop in modeled data is not reflected in the 
measured data due to the limitations of the sensor. It is important to 
note, that AQUASIM assumes ideal homogenization in all modeled 
compartments (liquid phase, headspace, and biofilm), therefore, in such 
low concentrations, the results may differ. 
Experimentally measured data followed the same trend as the data 
calculated from the model, and the differences were in the order of tens 
of ppm. Thus, the mathematical model satisfactorily described the fate 
of sulfur compounds in the microaerobic fermenter. Even though the 
experimental data showed a similar trend as was expected from the 
mathematical model, the real concentration of H2S in biogas was even 
lower for the gradual increase of stirring intensity. Apparently, under 
these conditions, microaeration is affected by yet another factor (e.g.,

3.5. Applicability of the gradually increasing stirring intensity in full scale 
Based on the results presented in this study, gradually increasing 
stirring intensity is an effective method for maintaining consistently low 
H2S concentration in microaerobic SBRs and intermittently stirred and/ 
or fed CSTRs. Reduced H2S fluctuations in the biogas will lead to the 
extension of the applicability of microaeration in these reactors and to 
the mitigation of the side effects of H2S presence in resulting biogas 
while burning it in cogeneration units. 
Moreover, when pure oxygen is used, microaeration can be used for 
the pre-treatment when biomethanation is to be applied. In this study, 
thanks to microaeration, the concentration of H2S was reduced from 
approx. 6000 ppm to approx. 40 ppm. Subsequent post-treatment on e. 
g., activated carbon or membranes would deal with only minor residual 
H2S concentration, leading to a longer lifetime of chosen technology, 
and will provide important cost savings. 
4. Conclusion 
We experimentally verified a new operational strategy for efficient 
microaeration in anaerobic fermenters with intermittent mixing which 
was previously suggested based on mathematical modelling. The strat­
egy was based on gradual increase of stirring speed during each feeding 
cycle of the fermenter. In this study, the optimal conditions were the 
slow start of the stirring (15 RPM) for two hours, and subsequent in­
crease of stirring intensity to 35 RPM for another 2 h and 10 min. It was 
shown that such strategy reduced the maximum H2S concentration in 
biogas from 6000 ppm (without microaeration) to less than 40 ppm 
compared to the peak concentrations of up to 120 ppm for RPM between 
15 and 55. As explained by the mathematical model, the reduction of 
H2S peaks resulted from the slowdown of H2S release from liquid, which 
provided more time for biological oxidation in the headspace at the 
beginning of each SBR cycle. 
Importantly, the strategy functioned without having any negative 
effect on anaerobic fermentation and did not require any extension of 
reaction time. Because the operational strategy proposed does not 
require additional equipment, it can be immediately implemented in 
industrial practice.
